newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia '97 early cocoa harvest seen low.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia '97 early cocoa harvest seen low.

text.p: Malaysia's mid-year cocoa harvest could be sharply lower due to extreme dry weather and lack of pesticide and fertiliser use, and the situation may not improve much for the rest of 1997, growers said on Wednesday.

"I think this will be a very difficult year for cocoa," Hong Ngit-Ming, deputy managing director of Teck Guan Perdana Bhd, a cocoa grower and grinder in Malaysia's eastern Sabah state, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The Malaysian Cocoa Board (MCB), the authority for cocoa in Malaysia, said it expects production to fall to around 122,000 tonnes this year, unchanged from the estimated 122,000 tonnes in 1996, and lower than the 131,000 tonnes produced in 1995.
But growers estimated an output of just below 100,000 tonnes for 1997.
"My guess is that it'll be around 90,000 plus to 100,000 tonnes," said Hong.
MCB officials were unavailable to comment on the projections made by the growers, which came after the board's estimates in December.

Growers in Sabah, Malaysia's largest cocoa producing state accounting for nearly 80 percent of the crop's national output, said rainfall in January this year was only about 10 percent of the same month last year.
According to records of Sabah cocoa grower Landquest Sdn Bhd, there has been just 32 mm of rain so far in January 1997, compared to the 332.7 mm recorded in January 1996.
"This is too dry for cocoa," said Anthony Tsen, managing director of the company, based in Sabah's prime cocoa cultivation area of Tawau.
Tsen said investments made in pesticides and fertilisers, especially by smallholders, were decreasing due to the expensive cost of such materials and low economies of scale presented by the crop.
He said cocoa farmers were also clearing out their plantations to switch to palm oil, Malaysia's most profitable crop.
"All this adds up to a bad outlook for the mid-year harvest between April and June," said Tsen.
"The year-end harvest also doesn't look promising because of the continued lower trend usually shown in production," he added.
The mid-year harvest usually produces about 60 percent of Malaysia's annual cocoa output while the year-end harvest between October and December accounts for around 30 to 35 percent.
The balance of five to 10 percent is achieved between the "lull periods" of January to March and July to September, growers said.
Tsen said he only obtained 1.33 tonnes of cocoa beans -- the crop's final product before grinding -- for January this year, compared to 10.54 tonnes in January 1996.
Imports of cocoa beans from Indonesia are expected to rise this year if demand for finished cocoa products such as powder, butter and paste, grew, local cocoa grinders said.
However, they said they could not put a figure on this.
"I have a production capacity of 20,000 tonnes but it doesn't mean I'll be grinding as much this year if I don't get the corresponding demand," said Teck Guan Perdana's Hong.
Local cocoa grinders said Indonesian beans were lower in quality compared with Malaysian beans but were often blended with the local product to achieve the quantities required.
